items.title: Predicting taste alteration in head and neck cancer patients using 3D transformer-based deep learning model
items.authorsShort: Neh H, MacRae DC, de Vette SPM, ... van Dijk LV.
items.summary: Altered taste is a common lasting side effect of radiotherapy for head and neck cancer. Using a prospective cohort of 972 patients, this study asked whether deep-learning models that read the full 3D dose distribution, planning CT and organ contours could predict moderate-to-severe taste alteration six months after treatment better than a conventional model built on mean dose to the oral cavity and parotid glands plus age. The transformer model matched but did not beat the conventional model (AUC 0.71 for both), while its attention maps pointed to the supraglottic and submandibular regions, suggesting where dose matters most for taste.
items.authors: Neh H, MacRae DC, de Vette SPM, van der Hoek L, van Ooijen PMA, Sijtsema NM, Langendijk JA, van Dijk LV.

items.title: Evaluating imputation methods for longitudinal clinical trajectories: Toxicities in head and neck cancer treatment
items.authorsShort: van der Hoek L, de Vette SPM, Neh H, ... van Dijk LV.
items.summary: Side-effect scores collected repeatedly during and after radiotherapy are often incomplete, and how the gaps are filled can change what a model learns. This study compared nine imputation methods, from simple carry-forward rules to deep learning, on four toxicities (dry mouth, swallowing difficulty, taste alteration and sticky saliva) recorded at 16 time points in 1,442 head and neck cancer patients. Most methods performed similarly, but the simplest ones were clearly worse, and the authors advise care in which patients are included when a dataset has many missing time points.
items.authors: van der Hoek L, de Vette SPM, Neh H, MacRae DC, Langendijk JA, Sijtsema NM, van Ooijen PMA, van der Schaaf A, van Dijk LV.

items.title: ImPartial: Multi-channel Whole-Cell Segmentation using Partial Annotations
items.authorsShort: Shrivastava G, Nadeem S.
items.summary: Outlining individual cells in pathology images normally requires dense, pixel-by-pixel labels that are slow and expensive to produce, especially for newer multiplexed imaging methods with varying channel layouts. ImPartial is a deep-learning framework that learns from sparse scribbles instead, adding a self-supervised task that quantizes and imputes image channels so the network learns structure without full labels. On benchmark multiplexed datasets and clinical brightfield immunohistochemistry slides it matched fully supervised models with far fewer annotations; code and data are released on GitHub.
items.authors: Shrivastava G, Nadeem S.

items.title: Long-term outcomes and patterns of failure in patients with thymic malignancies treated with surgery and radiation therapy
items.authorsShort: Icht O, Nardi-Agmon I, Thavendiranathan P, ... Hope A.
items.summary: Whether radiation around the time of surgery helps patients with thymic tumors has never been settled by a randomized trial. This retrospective study followed 360 patients treated surgically at a high-volume center between 2004 and 2021, about half of whom also received radiation. Recurrences were mostly in the pleura rather than in the irradiated field, tumor invasiveness (especially vascular invasion) was the strongest predictor of relapse, and a survival benefit from radiation appeared only after statistical adjustment — so the authors call for prospective testing.
items.authors: Icht O, Nardi-Agmon I, Thavendiranathan P, Keshavjee S, Agrawal A, Miro JM, Badran O, Liu G, Ye XY, Cho BCJ, Bezjak A, Hope A.

items.title: MSK's DP4All Initiative Advances Global Health Equity Goals by Bringing Digital Pathology Innovation to Low-Resource Settings
items.venue: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (institutional announcement)
items.summary: MSK announced Digital Pathology for All (DP4All), an initiative led by Saad Nadeem and colleagues that turns an ordinary smartphone camera attached to a microscope into a tool for digitizing and analyzing pathology slides. Grants from Global Cancer Research and Training, Stanford University, and MSK's ai-TDIF fund will support deployments at hospitals in Rwanda, Nigeria, and Tanzania, bringing AI-assisted pathology to settings that cannot afford conventional slide scanners.

items.title: Elected Vice Chair of ASTRO's Health Care Access and Community Engagement Council
items.summary: In ASTRO's 2026 elections, Gita Suneja was elected Vice Chair of the Health Care Access and Community Engagement Council, one of eight new officers joining the ASTRO Board of Directors and Nominating Committee. Her term begins September 29, 2026.

items.title: Chronic Hypertension Impairs Lymphatic Drainage in Deep Cervical Lymph Nodes
items.authorsShort: Xu K, Bhardwaj A, Koundal S, ... Georgiou TT
items.summary: Using imaging and fluid-transport modeling in rats, the team compared lymph drainage through the deep neck lymph nodes in normal animals and animals with chronic high blood pressure. Hypertensive animals showed simpler flow patterns and reduced flow through these nodes, indicating impaired drainage. Because these nodes help clear waste from the brain, the work suggests one way a common systemic condition may affect brain health.

items.title: Generative AI, foundation models and large language models in radiation therapy physics: Clinical applications, challenges, and future directions
items.authorsShort: Qi XS, Wang Y, Yang X, ... El Naqa IM
items.summary: This review surveys how generative AI, foundation models, and large language models are beginning to be used in radiation therapy physics, from analyzing medical images and automating routine tasks to supporting clinical decisions and streamlining workflows. The authors also lay out the main hurdles to safe adoption, including interpretability, data privacy, regulatory compliance, reproducibility, and AI 'hallucination', and offer guidance for medical physicists and clinicians navigating these tools.
items.authors: Qi XS, Wang Y, Yang X, Ren L, Liu W, Benedict SH, Xiao Y, Xing L, El Naqa IM.

items.title: Named a 2026 Fellow of the American Society for Radiation Oncology (FASTRO)
items.summary: ASTRO's 2026 class of Fellows includes Issam El Naqa of Moffitt Cancer Center. The FASTRO designation recognizes members whose contributions to research, education, patient care or service have had a lasting impact on radiation oncology.

items.title: Clinical implementation of automated IMRT/VMAT planning for lung cancer radiation therapy using the expedited constrained hierarchical optimization (ECHO) system
items.authorsShort: Jeong J, Huang Q, Zhou Y, ... Hong L
items.summary: This paper reports the routine clinical use at MSK of ECHO, an in-house automated treatment-planning system, for lung cancer radiotherapy. Since 2021-2023, 431 patients received ECHO-generated IMRT plans and 93 SBRT patients received ECHO-generated VMAT plans; the automated plans gave more consistent tumor coverage with comparable protection of healthy organs versus manually built plans. Optimization took about 33 minutes (IMRT) or 56 minutes (VMAT), saving roughly 1.5 hours of planner time per patient.
items.authors: Jeong J, Huang Q, Zhou Y, Yorke E, Lin E, Jhanwar G, Yang J, Pham H, Thor M, Wu AJ, Cervino L, Moran JM, Deasy JO, Zarepisheh M, Hong L.

items.title: Long-Term Changes in Physical Activity Among Cancer Survivors After Concurrent Chemoradiation Therapy: A Prospective Study
items.venue: International Journal of Radiation Oncology, Biology, Physics (Red Journal)
items.authorsShort: Zakharia A, Kabarriti R, Bodner WR, ... Ohri N
items.summary: A prospective study from Montefiore Einstein, led by Dr. Ohri as senior author, that followed cancer survivors over the long term after concurrent chemoradiation to measure how their physical activity changed. Understanding how activity levels recover (or fail to recover) after intensive treatment can help clinicians support survivors' fitness and quality of life.
items.flag: Summary based on title and bibliographic record only; abstract not reviewed.

items.title: Montefiore Einstein lung cancer team receives IASLC Cancer Care Team Award (Dr. Ohri named among honored clinicians)
items.summary: The International Association for the Study of Lung Cancer gave its Cancer Care Team Award to the Montefiore Einstein Comprehensive Cancer Center lung cancer team, the sole North American recipient, after a nomination from a patient who credited the team's coordinated, patient-centered approach. Dr. Nitin Ohri, Professor of Radiation Oncology, was specifically named among the clinicians honored.

items.title: A multi-toxicity deep learning approach for normal tissue complication probability modelling in head and neck cancer patients receiving radiotherapy
items.authorsShort: MacRae DC, van der Hoek L, de Vette SPM, ... van Dijk LV
items.summary: The team built a 3D deep-learning model that predicts five different radiotherapy side effects at once (such as swallowing problems and dry mouth) in head and neck cancer patients, using radiation dose maps and imaging from 1,418 patients. Predicting several toxicities together outperformed conventional models and single-toxicity deep learning models for dysphagia and xerostomia. Such models could help doctors tailor radiotherapy plans to reduce lasting side effects.
items.authors: MacRae DC, van der Hoek L, de Vette SPM, Neh H, Moreno AC, Fuller CD, Langendijk JA, Valdenegro-Toro MA, Sijtsema NM, van Ooijen PMA, van Dijk LV.

items.title: Yongxin Chen Awarded the IFAC's Manfred Thoma Medal
items.venue: Georgia Tech Daniel Guggenheim School of Aerospace Engineering (news)
items.summary: The International Federation of Automatic Control (IFAC) awarded Chen its Manfred Thoma Medal, which recognizes outstanding contributions to systems and control by a researcher under 40. The medal honors his work connecting stochastic control with optimal transport, with applications from drone swarms to artificial intelligence. He is the first Georgia Tech faculty member to receive it and will accept it at the IFAC World Congress in Busan, Korea, in August 2026.

items.title: Global Ovarian Cancer Research Consortium inaugural $1M AI Accelerator Grant (UK team member)
items.venue: Ovarian Cancer Action / Cancer Research UK Cambridge Institute
items.summary: An international team including Cambridge's Mireia Crispin received the first $1 million AI Accelerator Grant from the Global Ovarian Cancer Research Consortium, plus about $1 million in computing support from Microsoft's AI for Good Lab. The project will use AI to combine scans, lab results and genetic data from thousands of ovarian cancer patients across several countries to better predict survival and match patients to the treatments most likely to work.

items.title: Hanarth Fonds grant (EUR 493,593): AI-based lymph node-specific risk stratification to reduce post-chemoradiotherapy salvage complications in head and neck cancer
items.summary: Van Dijk (with ENT surgeon Inge Wegner, UMCG) received a Hanarth Fonds award of about EUR 494,000 to develop AI models that predict which individual lymph nodes still harbor cancer after chemoradiotherapy for head and neck cancer. Today 60-70% of salvage neck operations find no residual tumor, yet the surgery carries real complications. The tool, combining CT, PET and MRI with deep learning, aims to spare patients unnecessary surgery while treating high-risk nodes earlier.

items.title: Conversation with Prof. Saad Nadeem, Memorial Sloan Kettering (Thought Leaders episode)
items.summary: In this interview, Nadeem discusses DeepLIIF, his lab's open-source AI tool for quantifying immunohistochemistry stains, and the DP4All initiative. The conversation focuses on making digital and computational pathology tools accessible across healthcare settings with very different resource levels.

items.title: SMMILe enables accurate spatial quantification in digital pathology using multiple-instance learning
items.authorsShort: Gao Z, Mao A, Dong Y, ... Crispin-Ortuzar M
items.summary: The team built SMMILe, an AI method that reads whole-slide pathology images and not only classifies the slide (e.g., tumor type) but also maps precisely where within the tissue the relevant features are. Tested on 3,850 slides across six cancer types, it matched or beat existing methods at classification while giving far better spatial maps, which could make AI pathology tools more trustworthy and useful to pathologists.
items.authors: Gao Z, Mao A, Dong Y, Clayton H, Wu J, Liu J, Wang C, He K, Gong T, Li C, Crispin-Ortuzar M.

items.title: Professor Caroline Moosmüller Wins Junior Principal Investigator Award from 2025 ASciNA Awards
items.summary: Moosmüller received the 2025 ASciNA (Austrian Scientists and Scholars in North America) Junior Principal Investigator Award, described as one of the most prestigious honors for Austrian researchers working in North America and carrying a EUR 10,000 prize. The award recognized her paper on linearized Wasserstein dimensionality reduction, a mathematical method for simplifying complex, high-dimensional data.

items.title: Radiation oncologist Zeno Gouw studies primer-shot radiotherapy: a smarter way to treat with radiation
items.summary: An NKI feature profiles Gouw's research on 'primer-shot' radiotherapy, which delivers a first dose of radiation, waits about three weeks for dead tumor cells to clear and blood flow in the tumor to improve, and then delivers the remaining treatment. The idea is that better-oxygenated tumors respond more strongly to the later radiation, potentially making treatment more effective without adding dose.

items.title: Dr Jamie Dean receives Medical Research Council Career Development Award
items.summary: Jamie Dean was awarded a Medical Research Council Career Development Award fellowship worth roughly 2.1 million pounds, a UK award that lets early-career scientists lead their own research programs. His project, 'Revealing and Overcoming Mechanisms of Microglia-Mediated Radiotherapy Resistance in Diffuse Midline Glioma', will study how brain immune cells (microglia) help a deadly childhood brain tumor resist radiotherapy, with the aim of finding ways to make treatment more effective.

items.title: Named to the 2025 Class of ASTRO Fellows (FASTRO)
items.summary: The American Society for Radiation Oncology named Gita Suneja a Fellow of ASTRO, an honor recognizing members who have made significant contributions to the field through research, education, patient care or service to the society.

items.title: Association of artificial intelligence-screened interstitial lung disease with radiation pneumonitis in locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer
items.authorsShort: Xing S, Elguindi S, Shaverdian N, ... Thor M
items.summary: Pre-existing interstitial lung disease (scarring of the lung tissue) is thought to raise the risk of radiation pneumonitis, but it is often subtle and under-recognized on planning scans. This study used an artificial-intelligence tool to screen planning CT scans of patients with locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer for interstitial lung disease and examined how these AI-detected findings relate to the development of radiation pneumonitis. Automatically flagging at-risk lungs before treatment could help clinicians tailor radiotherapy to reduce lung injury.

items.title: Dose accumulation over the treatment course including setup and range uncertainty for proton therapy of esophageal and lung cancer patients
items.authorsShort: Taasti VT, Hattu D, Berbée M, ... Canters R
items.summary: Proton therapy is highly sensitive to changes in a patient's anatomy, so the dose actually delivered over weeks of treatment can differ from the plan. This study builds a method that adds up the delivered dose across repeat CT scans while accounting for setup and proton-range uncertainty, and a quality-assurance check for the image-deformation step. Tested on 40 esophageal and lung cancer patients, it showed why anatomical changes must be tracked and which registration settings work best for each site.
items.authors: Taasti VT, Hattu D, Berbée M, de Ruysscher D, Canters R.

items.title: Daily proton dose re-calculation on deep-learning corrected cone-beam computed tomography scans
items.authorsShort: Vestergaard CD, Muren LP, Elstrøm UV, ... Taasti VT
items.summary: Adaptive proton therapy needs a CT-quality image every day, but the daily cone-beam CT is too noisy for proton dose calculation. The team trained a 3D deep-learning network to convert cone-beam scans of prostate cancer patients into synthetic CTs and checked them across all 39 treatment sessions. The synthetic images matched real CT values, kept proton range errors under about 2 mm, and gave accurate target coverage, making them a practical basis for adapting proton plans day to day.
items.authors: Vestergaard CD, Muren LP, Elstrøm UV, Stolarczyk L, Nørrevang O, Petersen SE, Taasti VT.

items.title: 2025 ASTRO-AstraZeneca Small Cell Lung Cancer Therapy Challenge awardee
items.summary: ASTRO and AstraZeneca selected Nitin Ohri of Albert Einstein College of Medicine as an awardee of their 2025 Small Cell Lung Cancer Therapy Challenge for his proposal on chemoradiotherapy optimized for immunotherapy in limited-stage small cell lung cancer.

items.title: Angiogenic and immune predictors of neoadjuvant axitinib response in renal cell carcinoma with venous tumour thrombus
items.authorsShort: Wray R, Paverd H, Machado I, ... Jones JO
items.summary: In some kidney cancers the tumor grows into the major veins, making surgery risky; the NAXIVA trial had shown the drug axitinib can shrink this thrombus before surgery in about a third of patients. Using pathology, immune profiling, blood cytokines and RNA sequencing from trial samples, the team found responders have denser tumor blood vessels and a characteristic rise in growth factors during treatment. A machine-learning model combining these features predicted response with high accuracy, pointing toward better selection of patients for this approach.
items.authors: Wray R, Paverd H, Machado I, Barbieri J, Easita F, Edwards AR, Gallagher FA, Mendichovszky IA, Mitchell TJ, de la Roche M, Shields JD, Ursprung S, Wallis L, Warren AY, Welsh SJ, Crispin-Ortuzar M, Stewart GD, Jones JO, NAXIVA Study Group.

items.title: Pregnancy-related proteins in tumors linked to worse survival in female lung cancer patients
items.venue: Memorial Sloan Kettering — In the News
items.summary: MSK reported on a study led by Jung Hun Oh showing that lung cancers can switch on pregnancy-specific glycoprotein genes, which normally help a fetus evade the mother's immune system, and that patients whose tumors do so fare worse. Co-authors include Rena Elkin and Corey Weistuch, also lab alumni.

items.summary: PathPresenter announced a partnership with Memorial Sloan Kettering to bring DeepLIIF, the AI tool created by Saad Nadeem's lab for virtual staining and quantification of immunohistochemistry, into its digital pathology platform for research use.

items.summary: A University of Cambridge feature profiles Mireia Crispin ahead of her Cambridge Festival talk, describing her work using AI to detect and understand cancer earlier and her role as Chief Digital Officer of the spin-out 52 North Health.

items.title: Short-course radiation therapy effective for endometrial cancer (SAVE trial press release)
items.summary: University of Utah Health announced results of the SAVE trial led by Gita Suneja, showing that a two-visit course of vaginal cuff brachytherapy after surgery for early endometrial cancer matched the standard three-to-five-visit schedule on quality of life and cancer control, with fewer trips for patients.

items.title: Stereotactic Body Radiotherapy vs Sorafenib Alone in Hepatocellular Carcinoma: The NRG Oncology/RTOG 1112 Phase 3 Randomized Clinical Trial
items.authorsShort: Dawson LA, Winter KA, Knox JJ, ... Crane CH
items.summary: This multicenter phase 3 trial asked whether adding stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) before the drug sorafenib helps patients with advanced liver cancer. Among 177 patients, median survival rose from 12.3 to 15.8 months with SBRT, and progression-free survival improved from 5.5 to 9.2 months. The survival gain was clinically meaningful but did not reach statistical significance on the primary analysis, in part because enrollment stopped early when standard drug therapy changed.
items.authors: Dawson LA, Winter KA, Knox JJ, Zhu AX, Krishnan S, Guha C, Kachnic LA, Gillin MT, Hong TS, Craig TD, Williams TM, Hosni A, Chen E, Noonan AM, Koay EJ, Sinha R, Lock MI, Ohri N, Dorth JA, Delouya G, Swaminath A, Moughan J, Crane CH.

items.title: Intricacies of human-AI interaction in dynamic decision-making for precision oncology
items.authorsShort: Niraula D, Cuneo KC, Dinov ID, ... El Naqa I
items.summary: AI tools can suggest how to adapt radiotherapy as a patient's cancer responds, but they are imperfect, and clinicians may trust them too much or too little. In a study of adaptive radiotherapy decisions for lung and liver cancer, the team found that how clinicians use AI advice depends on many things at once: their prior beliefs, the patient's condition, the disease site, how transparent the model is, and the model's own biases. Some clinicians ignore the AI, others weigh it case by case, and most will change course when they see a recommendation clearly helps the patient.
items.authors: Niraula D, Cuneo KC, Dinov ID, Gonzalez BD, Jamaluddin JB, Jin JJ, Luo Y, Matuszak MM, Ten Haken RK, Bryant AK, Dilling TJ, Dykstra MP, Frakes JM, Liveringhouse CL, Miller SR, Mills MN, Palm RF, Regan SN, Rishi A, Torres-Roca JF, Yu HM, El Naqa I.

items.title: Biological correlates associated with high-risk breast cancer patients identified using a computational method
items.authorsShort: Oh JH, Pareja F, Elkin R, ... Deasy JO
items.summary: Using a computational method that integrates several kinds of molecular data, the team had previously found a group of breast cancers with unusually poor outcomes. Here they characterize what makes that group different: its tumors score high on three separate hypoxia (low-oxygen) signatures and contain fewer tumor-infiltrating immune cells. The result suggests this hidden high-risk subgroup is driven by a distinct biology that could be targeted.
items.authors: Oh JH, Pareja F, Elkin R, Xu K, Norton L, Deasy JO.

items.title: Moffitt study shows AI boosts efficacy of cancer treatment, but doctors remain key
items.summary: Moffitt Cancer Center highlighted El Naqa's Nature Communications study of how clinicians interact with AI recommendations when adapting radiotherapy. The release quotes him on the finding that AI can sharpen decisions from complex data while clinicians' judgment remains essential to safe, personalized cancer care.

items.title: Normal tissue complication probability model predicting taste impairment in head and neck cancer patients: Evaluating the taste bud bearing tongue mucosa as a predictor
items.authorsShort: Neh H, de Vette SPM, Stoffers RH, ... van Dijk LV
items.summary: Loss of taste is a common and under-appreciated side effect of radiotherapy for head and neck cancer. In 691 patients, the team tested whether the radiation dose to a new, taste-specific structure (the taste-bud-bearing tongue mucosa) predicts taste loss better than the dose to the whole oral cavity. It did not: the simpler oral-cavity dose worked just as well, a useful negative result for how toxicity models are built.
items.authors: Neh H, de Vette SPM, Stoffers RH, Zhou G, van Ooijen PMA, Sijtsema NM, Brouwer CL, Langendijk JA, van Dijk LV.

items.title: Randomized Evaluation of the PET-Adjusted IMRT for NSCLC Trial (REPAINT)
items.venue: International Journal of Radiation Oncology, Biology, Physics (Red Journal)
items.authorsShort: Ohri N, Bodner WR, Kabarriti R, ... Halmos B
items.summary: Standard radiotherapy for locally advanced lung cancer gives every tumor the same dose. This randomized trial tested a personalized, de-intensified approach that uses each tumor's PET-measured metabolic volume to lower the dose to smaller lesions and shorten treatment to 20 sessions. Across 50 patients, survival and tumor control were similar in both arms, while severe lymphocyte depletion was less common with the dose-painted approach, suggesting the strategy is safe to study further.
items.authors: Ohri N, Bodner WR, Kabarriti R, Shankar V, Gucalp R, Cheng H, Halmos B.

items.title: Clinical validation of a prognostic preclinical magnetic resonance imaging biomarker for radiotherapy outcome in head-and-neck cancer
items.authorsShort: Winter RM, Boeke S, Leibfarth S, ... Thorwarth D
items.summary: An imaging biomarker first discovered in animal studies, based on a band of diffusion-MRI values marking radiation-resistant tumor subvolumes, was retrained and tested in 31 patients with head and neck cancer. The size of these high-risk subvolumes before treatment strongly predicted outcome three years later, outperforming tumor volume and average diffusion values. If confirmed in larger cohorts, the marker could guide MRI-guided, response-adapted radiotherapy.
items.authors: Winter RM, Boeke S, Leibfarth S, Habrich J, Clasen K, Nikolaou K, Zips D, Thorwarth D.

items.title: Short-Course Adjuvant Vaginal Cuff Brachytherapy in Early Endometrial Cancer Compared with Standard of Care (SAVE): A Randomized Clinical Trial
items.authorsShort: Suneja G, et al.
items.summary: After surgery for early endometrial cancer, many women receive internal radiation to the top of the vagina over three to five visits. The SAVE trial, the first US multicenter randomized study of this question, compared a two-visit course with standard schedules. Quality of life one month and one year after treatment was no worse with the shorter course, side effects were similar or fewer, and cancer control in the vagina was 96% in both groups at about two years.

items.title: Optimizing the delivery of radiotherapy with artificial intelligence
items.authorsShort: Katsoulakis E, El Naqa I.
items.summary: This review surveys how artificial intelligence and machine learning are being used across radiation oncology — automating contouring, adapting treatments to anatomical change, calculating dose, quality assurance and predicting outcomes. It examines why clinical deployment still lags behind the technology's promise, covering technical, practical, ethical and legal hurdles, and looks ahead to generative AI and foundation models.
items.authors: Katsoulakis E, El Naqa I.

items.title: Leave No Data Behind: Exploring a new paradigm in oncology with foundation models and large language models
items.authorsShort: Corso F, Zec A, Favali M, ... Prelaj A.
items.summary: A narrative review proposing that oncology AI should 'leave no data behind' — combining medical imaging, electronic health records and molecular profiles in foundation models and large language models. The authors weigh the evidence that such broad data integration produces clinically meaningful results and lay out the main challenges still to be solved.
items.authors: Corso F, Zec A, Favali M, Ligero M, Hilgers L, Invernizzi LM, Mazzeo L, Morales AM, Müller-Franzes GA, Prata Machado I, Busch F, Mišković V, Trovò F, Proto C, Lo Russo G, Occhipinti M, Brambilla M, Beninato T, Halabi S, Garassino MC, Pedrocchi ALG, Pellat A, Adams L, Calderaro J, Truhn D, Delaloge S, Vibert J, Lipkova J, Koopman M, Perez-Lopez R, Crispin-Ortuzar M, Kather JN, Prelaj A.

items.title: A multimodal murmuration for immunotherapy
items.authorsShort: Perez-Lopez R, Crispin-Ortuzar M.
items.summary: A News & Views commentary in Nature Medicine on a study showing that combining many patient-level biomarkers from different data types improves predictions of who will respond to cancer immunotherapy. The authors single out generalizability — whether such multimodal models hold up across patient populations and care settings — as the key remaining challenge.
items.authors: Perez-Lopez R, Crispin-Ortuzar M.

items.title: ALPaCA: Adapting Llama for Pathology Context Analysis to enable slide-level question answering
items.authorsShort: Gao Z, He K, Su W, ... Crispin-Ortuzar M.
items.summary: ALPaCA adapts the Llama large language model to answer questions about entire gigapixel pathology whole-slide images rather than small regions of interest. Trained on more than 35,000 slides with curated descriptions and over 340,000 question–answer pairs, it supports slide-level assessment across many cancer types and tissue sites.
items.authors: Gao Z, He K, Su W, Pang X, Machado IP, Jimenez-Linan M, Rous B, Wang C, Li C, McGough W, Gao S, Zhang D, Gong T, Lu MY, Mahmood F, Feng M, Li C, Crispin-Ortuzar M.

items.title: A generalizable foundation model for analysis of human brain MRI
items.authorsShort: Tak D, Garomsa BA, Zapaishchykova A, ... Kann BH
items.summary: Introduces BrainIAC, a foundation model that learns general-purpose representations from unlabeled brain MRI scans and can be adapted to many downstream clinical tasks. Trained and validated on nearly 49,000 brain MRIs, it outperformed task-specific supervised models and other pretrained models.

items.title: Longitudinal Risk Prediction for Pediatric Glioma with Temporal Deep Learning
items.authorsShort: Tak D, Garomsa BA, Zapaishchykova A, ... Kann BH
items.summary: A self-supervised temporal deep-learning approach reads a child's serial MRI scans to predict the risk of glioma recurrence over time, trained by learning to put scans in chronological order. The aim is to individualize long-term imaging surveillance, which today is applied uniformly to almost all children regardless of risk.

items.title: Thymic Composition Predicts Radiation Pneumonitis in Locally Advanced NSCLC
items.authorsShort: Chaunzwa TL, Krishnan G, Book AJ, ... Shaverdian N
items.summary: Using pretreatment CT scans from the RTOG 0617 trial and from MSK patients with locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer, the study shows that percent thymic tissue — an interpretable, automatically segmented measure of residual thymus — is associated with severe radiation pneumonitis after chemoradiotherapy. Thymic health may help explain toxicity risk that lung dose alone does not.

items.authorsShort: Nitin Ohri
items.summary: ASTRO and AstraZeneca named three winning projects in the 2025 Small Cell Lung Cancer Therapy Challenge, with up to $750,000 awarded across them. Nitin Ohri's project, COILSS (Chemoradiotherapy Optimized for Immunotherapy for Limited Stage Small Cell Lung Cancer), aims to optimize chemoradiation for use with immunotherapy in limited-stage disease.

items.title: ASciNA Award 2025, Junior Principal Investigator category
items.authorsShort: Caroline Moosmüller
items.summary: The ASciNA network and Austria's Federal Ministry for Women, Science and Research presented Caroline Moosmüller (UNC Chapel Hill) with the 2025 ASciNA Award in the Junior Principal Investigator category. The award recognizes her work on analyzing high-dimensional data with the LOT Wassmap method, with applications to cancer research.
